name: Asking Data Questions in Plain Language
title: Asking Data Questions in Plain Language
answer: Asking data questions in plain language covers the practice of querying structured datasets, tables, and documents using natural language instead of formal query code. It sits within quantitative analysis and reproducible work because the goal is to let analysts, researchers, and domain experts frame questions in their own words and receive answers with the underlying data operations visible. The scope includes translating questions into SQL, dataframe operations, or retrieval steps, and checking that the result matches the intent of the question. It also covers follow-up questions, clarification, and the ability to trace how an answer was produced.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Asking data questions in plain language covers the practice of querying structured datasets, tables, and documents using natural language instead of formal query code. It sits within quantitative analysis and reproducible work because the goal is to let analysts, researchers, and domain experts frame questions in their own words and receive answers with the underlying data operations visible. The scope includes translating questions into SQL, dataframe operations, or retrieval steps, and checking that the result matches the intent of the question. It also covers follow-up questions, clarification, and the ability to trace how an answer was produced.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on ordinary analytical infrastructure: relational databases, columnar stores, data warehouses, and notebooks that hold tabular data. A plain language layer typically sits on top of a query engine, a schema or data dictionary, and sometimes a vector index over table and column descriptions. Compute needs are modest compared with large generative model training; most of the cost is in model inference, query execution, and caching of common question patterns. The site's library of research papers and extracted claims can serve as a test corpus for evaluating whether a plain language answer matches documented findings.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core method is to parse a natural language question into a structured representation, usually SQL or a dataframe expression, then execute it against the data and return the result with the generated query shown. Systems use a language model to propose candidate queries, a schema-aware prompt that includes table names, column names, and sample values, and a validation step that checks syntax and row counts. Reproducible work requires that the generated query, the data version, and the model version are all recorded, so another analyst can rerun the same question and get the same answer. When the question is ambiguous, the method includes asking for clarification rather than guessing.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on data access, provenance, and silent errors. A plain language interface must enforce the same row-level and column-level permissions as the underlying database, so a user cannot phrase a question in a way that bypasses access controls. The main risk is a confident wrong answer: the model may generate valid SQL that answers a different question than the one asked, or it may join tables incorrectly. Governance therefore requires showing the generated query, the returned rows, and a confidence or verification signal, and keeping an audit log of questions, queries, and data snapshots. The site's practice of linking to original papers rather than a search tool reflects the same principle: the source of a claim must be inspectable.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward tighter coupling between plain language questions and reproducible analysis pipelines, where a question can be turned into a reusable, versioned query or notebook cell. Future systems are likely to support multi-step questions across several tables and documents, with explicit uncertainty about which interpretation was chosen. There is also movement toward smaller, task-specific models that run inside a data warehouse or notebook, reducing the need to send sensitive schema and data to external services. Over time, plain language asking may become a standard front end for data catalogues and evidence synthesis, but the generated code and data lineage will remain the record of what was actually asked and answered.
